0eec71ac6650.headline: David Fincher's New Cliff Booth Film Draws Fire Over Alleged Heavy Use of AI Imagery
body: Critics and film fans are accusing director David Fincher's new movie, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," of leaning heavily on sloppy AI-generated imagery, according to Futurism. The complaints began Thursday on film-focused corners of X after early screenings.

Filmmaker and YouTube critic Patrick Tomasso, who often covers the technical side of movies, said he left the screening "completely gutted." He described the AI use as some of the most blatant he has seen in a studio film. A user who says they work in VFX also called the amount of AI astounding.

Tomasso listed what he considers telltale signs: faces changing mid-scene, odd physics, garbled fine lines, full-body performance swaps, and AI-looking signs, fire and traffic. He also pointed to the trailer, where two people ride a wagon backwards, seemingly holding reins for horses that are actually behind them.

The accusations sting because of Fincher's reputation. The director of Fight Club, Se7en and The Social Network is known for perfectionism and for subtle, invisible visual effects that polish an image without viewers noticing. Futurism notes the warning signs were there: in March, Bloomberg reported he was using AI post-production tools from Ben Affleck's company InterPositive, and he used generative AI to tidy shot compositions in the new 4K restoration of Se7en.

Fincher also gave the Los Angeles Times an interview that landed at an awkward moment. He called himself "not a Luddite" and defended AI's place in filmmaking, asking whether people really want to freeze an art form that is only about a hundred years old. The claims so far come from critics and online commenters, and the article does not include a response from the studio.
0eec71ac6650.summary: Early viewers say David Fincher's "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is packed with obvious AI imagery. Fincher, who has defended AI in filmmaking, now faces a backlash from critics and VFX workers.
0eec71ac6650.pixel_take: Fincher is famous for demanding 100 takes of everything. Apparently the horses got a lighter schedule and ended up behind the wagon.
0eec71ac6650.why_it_matters: Hollywood is testing how much generative AI audiences will tolerate, and visible glitches in a big-name studio film raise the reputational risk. Studios chasing lower post-production costs may find that viewers, and the artists who make the films, push back hard on quality and authenticity.
key_points: Critics and a self-described VFX worker allege obvious AI flaws in Fincher's new film.
Cited problems include shifting faces, garbled details and a trailer shot with horses behind the wagon.
Fincher previously used AI tools and defended AI in an LA Times interview.

e6ea1336b4c9.headline: Lagarde Warns Europe Could Lose Grip on Tokenized Assets as a €1 Billion Digital Bond Settles
body: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has warned that Europe risks losing control of the fast-growing market for tokenized assets, and she called for common rules across the EU, according to CoinDesk.

The warning came as the EU's new blockchain-based settlement system handled a digital bond transaction worth 1 billion euros, roughly $1.1 billion. The material available does not say who issued the bond or give further details about the deal.

Tokenization means representing traditional financial assets, such as bonds, as digital tokens on a blockchain so they can be issued, traded and settled electronically. Supporters say this can speed up settlement and cut back-office costs. The catch is that if every country, platform and regulator plays by different rules, the market can fragment into a patchwork.

Lagarde's message, as reported, is that Europe should set shared standards before others set them for it. Central banks care about this because settlement systems sit at the plumbing level of finance, and whoever runs the plumbing has a lot of say over how money flows.

The size of the transaction is a notable signal. A billion-euro bond is far from a small experiment, and it suggests that regulated institutions are testing blockchain settlement with serious sums. Still, the source material gives no broader market figures, so it is too early to say how big the tokenized market in Europe really is.
e6ea1336b4c9.summary: ECB President Christine Lagarde called for common EU rules on tokenized assets, warning Europe could lose control of the market, as a new blockchain settlement system processed a €1 billion digital bond.
e6ea1336b4c9.pixel_take: Lagarde wants Europe to write the rulebook before someone else hands it a copy. A billion-euro bond on a blockchain is a big test, not a toy.
e6ea1336b4c9.why_it_matters: Tokenized bonds could change how debt is issued and settled, which affects costs for issuers and eventually returns for investors. Shared EU rules would shape which platforms win and whether Europe keeps control over its financial infrastructure.
key_points: Lagarde called for common EU rules on tokenized assets.
She warned Europe could lose control of the growing market.
The EU's blockchain settlement system handled a €1 billion ($1.1 billion) digital bond.

bc4bf2d54934.headline: Stocks Hit a Correction Before Thanksgiving, and Some Are Already in a Bear Market
body: US stocks are heading into the Thanksgiving holiday in correction territory, according to MarketWatch, with some stocks already sliding into a full bear market. The timing is awkward, as the crucial holiday shopping period is right around the corner.

A quick refresher on the jargon: a correction is generally defined as a drop of 10% or more from a recent peak, while a bear market means a decline of 20% or more. So the market is, in effect, in a bad mood, and parts of it are in a much worse one.

The source material is thin on specifics, so we can't say which stocks are hurting most or how far prices have fallen. What the teaser does make clear is the concern: weak markets arriving just before the busiest stretch of the retail calendar.

Why does that matter? Holiday shopping is a big moment for retailers and for consumer-facing companies in general. Falling stock prices can dent household wealth and confidence, and people who feel poorer tend to spend more cautiously. That is a general pattern rather than a guarantee, but it explains why investors are watching this stretch so closely.

For everyday investors, corrections are common and often temporary, though no one can promise how long this one lasts. The usual advice still applies: keep your time horizon in mind, avoid panic decisions, and don't let a red screen talk you into buying things you didn't need on Black Friday either.
bc4bf2d54934.summary: US stocks are in correction territory heading into Thanksgiving, with some already in a bear market, MarketWatch reports, raising concerns about timing just ahead of the key holiday shopping season.
bc4bf2d54934.pixel_take: Stocks picked the perfect moment to go on sale. Just not the kind of sale anyone wants to line up for at 5 a.m.
bc4bf2d54934.why_it_matters: Market declines can chip away at investor confidence and household wealth, which may influence how freely consumers spend during the key holiday season. Retailers and the broader economy lean heavily on that period, so market mood matters beyond portfolios.
key_points: Stocks are in correction territory heading into Thanksgiving, per MarketWatch.
Some stocks have already fallen into a bear market.
The slump comes just before the crucial holiday shopping period.

ff7f5aa594da.headline: Judge Approves $7 Billion Roundup Settlement, Aiming to Weed Out Tens of Thousands of Cancer Lawsuits
body: A judge has approved a $7 billion settlement in a nationwide class-action lawsuit over claims that Roundup caused cancer, according to The New York Times. The ruling is expected to end tens of thousands of lawsuits from people who say the product caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The material available gives only the headline outline of the deal, so many specifics, such as how the money will be divided and how claimants will be paid, were not part of the information we reviewed. We are not going to guess at them.

What the ruling does signal is a potential finish line for one of the longest-running product-liability fights in corporate America. Mass litigation like this can drag on for years, with each case demanding its own lawyers, experts and court time. A single class-action settlement approved by a judge is a way to swap that sprawl for one big, defined number.

For companies, that kind of certainty is often the point. Investors tend to dislike open-ended legal exposure because it is hard to price, and a fixed sum, even a very large one, can be easier to model than thousands of unpredictable verdicts. For plaintiffs, a settlement trades the chance of a bigger courtroom win for a more predictable path to compensation.

The approval is a significant step, though the practical effects will depend on how the settlement is carried out and how many claimants are covered. Still, a $7 billion price tag shows how costly a sprawling health-claims fight can get, even when the underlying claims are contested.
ff7f5aa594da.summary: A judge approved a $7 billion nationwide class-action settlement over claims Roundup caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a ruling expected to end tens of thousands of lawsuits, The New York Times reports.
ff7f5aa594da.pixel_take: Seven billion dollars is a hefty price for a legal weed-whacking, but when the lawsuits number in the tens of thousands, even the lawn of litigation needs a serious trim.
ff7f5aa594da.why_it_matters: A settlement of this size can turn open-ended legal risk into a known cost, which matters for how investors value companies facing mass litigation. It also shows how expensive product-liability fights can become, a lesson for any industry selling widely used consumer or farm products.
key_points: A judge approved a $7 billion nationwide class-action settlement over Roundup cancer claims.
The ruling is expected to end tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Payout details were not available in the material reviewed.

de821aa0f1a3.headline: UN Talks on 'Killer Robots' End With a Promise to Keep Talking, Not a Treaty
body: A United Nations conference in Geneva has failed to agree on starting negotiations for legally binding rules on autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots." According to Al Jazeera, the 128 parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) instead agreed on Saturday to "elaborate" on a possible accord by 2028.

The week-long meeting followed last month's agreement by nearly 100 countries that binding rules should be adopted swiftly. But the CCW works by consensus, so one objection is enough to water down a deal. Reuters reported that overnight haggling over the final wording continued after Russian objections to procedural rules forced some formal meetings to be cancelled.

Diplomats cited by Politico and The Guardian said the US, Russia, Israel, the UK, South Korea, Japan and Turkiye resisted binding regulation. Supporters of a new convention reportedly included the EU, NATO member states, Ukraine, China and Iran. Major military powers argue that existing humanitarian law is already enough, and they prefer flexible, non-binding frameworks or longer timelines.

The semantics were telling. Swiss chair Julien Thoeni said some countries rejected the word "negotiate," so the text speaks of "elaboration" of an instrument. A diplomat from a supporting country told Reuters the result was "disappointing but could have been much worse."

The UN defines lethal autonomous weapons as systems that can identify, select and engage targets, resulting in loss of life, without human intervention. Not all of them use AI, though AI can amplify the legal and ethical concerns. AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine, Sudan and Middle East conflicts, according to the report.

Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of about 300 organisations, called the mandate watered down and said it offers no clear route to binding rules. Its director, Nicole van Rooijen, told AFP that delay puts civilians at risk. The Red Cross's Georgia Hinds called life-and-death decisions made by algorithm a moral red line.
de821aa0f1a3.summary: UN talks in Geneva failed to launch treaty negotiations on autonomous weapons, settling on 'elaborating' an accord by 2028 after resistance from major arms producers. Rights groups called the outcome disappointing.
de821aa0f1a3.why_it_matters: As militaries pour money into AI and autonomous systems, the lack of binding rules leaves defense tech largely unconstrained. That shapes the outlook for defense contractors, AI developers and regulators, and raises questions about liability and accountability when machines make lethal decisions.
key_points: The 128 CCW parties agreed only to 'elaborate' on a possible accord by 2028, not to negotiate a binding ban.
The US, Russia, Israel and other major military powers reportedly resisted binding rules.
Rights groups and the Red Cross warn that delay puts civilians at risk and crosses ethical lines.

beda3751c55d.headline: Army Plans to Detonate Lead Azide Anyway, Despite Court's Indefinite Pause
body: The U.S. Army says it intends to go ahead with the detonation of lead azide, even though a federal court ordered an indefinite pause, according to new court filings reported by The Hill on November 22, 2026.

The Army's route around the order is the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion. Per the teaser, the filings invoke that exclusion as the basis for proceeding, which suggests the service believes the court's pause does not apply to work it classifies as an emergency.

The material available is thin. It does not say where the lead azide is located, how much is involved, when the detonation would happen, or who brought the case. It also does not lay out the Army's full reasoning beyond the exclusion, so those details remain unconfirmed.

Some general context helps. Lead azide is a well-known primary explosive, used to set off other explosives, and it is sensitive and hazardous to handle. Agencies often argue that disposing of unstable materials is urgent, while courts weigh that against procedural and environmental requirements.

The standoff shows a familiar tension: when a government agency claims an emergency exception, judges and challengers may question whether the situation truly qualifies. What happens next will likely depend on how the court responds to the Army's filings.
beda3751c55d.summary: The Army says it will move ahead with detonating lead azide despite a federal court's indefinite pause, citing an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion, according to new court filings.
beda3751c55d.why_it_matters: Disputes over whether agencies can invoke emergency exceptions to bypass court orders test the limits of government authority and legal oversight. Outcomes can shape costs, liability and timelines for federal projects, which ultimately involve taxpayer money.
key_points: The Army plans to proceed with lead azide detonation despite a court-ordered indefinite pause.
It cites the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion, per new court filings.
Key details such as location, timing and the plaintiffs were not provided.

31c336541238.headline: Banks to AI Agents: Stay Out of Our Vaults, and Any Mistakes Are Your Problem
body: Major US banks are moving to block third-party AI agents from logging into customer accounts, and they are making clear that customers carry the risk if a bot goes wrong, according to Wired. Wells Fargo's updated customer agreement, which takes effect Tuesday, states that using any AI agent is "AT YOUR OWN RISK."

Wells Fargo is not alone. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with a customer's credentials. The same day, Bank of America warned customers not to share login details with agents. Citibank and PNC have also added agent warnings to their terms.

The fight goes beyond banking. Wired reports that Amazon blocked Meta's Muse, one of the most widely used agents, from making purchases on its platform, and United announced that personal bots will be blocked from buying flights on a traveler's behalf.

Experts quoted by Wired say the banks are playing defense. Forrester analyst Sucharita Kodali notes that most people don't even know what agents are, and she sees banks as risk-averse by nature, worried about transaction security and automated withdrawals that could hurt account holders. Marketing professor Kacy Kim argues that consumers authorize goals, not every click, so some will feel it is unfair to be blamed for an agent's errors. She doesn't expect the new terms to scare off committed early adopters.

The liability puzzle is murky. University of Virginia professor Luca Cian offers a hypothetical in which an agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens. The retailer says it filled a valid order, the AI builder says it only supplied software and warned of mistakes, and now the bank is also stepping back. American Express is the exception so far: it has said some agent errors, such as ordering too much of an item, may eventually be eligible for reimbursement if the retailer won't refund you.

Meanwhile, banks are building their own bots. Wells Fargo's generative AI assistant has been used over a billion times, Bank of America revamped its EricaAssist agent for employees, and Citigroup launched an internal agent development platform. As Cian puts it, banks are locking the door to outside agents while building their own.
31c336541238.summary: Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citi and PNC are restricting or warning against third-party AI agents, putting the risk of bot errors on customers while building their own AI tools, Wired reports.
31c336541238.pixel_take: Banks have told your AI agent the vault is closed, the chickens are yours, and the in-house bot is, coincidentally, open for business.
31c336541238.why_it_matters: If you let an AI agent use your bank login, you may have little recourse when it errs, and sharing credentials could breach your account terms. The shift also shows incumbents moving to control who gets to automate money, which will shape how agentic commerce develops.
key_points: Wells Fargo's new terms say using any AI agent is at the customer's own risk; JPMorgan bans agents using your credentials.
Bank of America, Citibank and PNC have issued warnings, while Amazon and United are also blocking shopping bots.
American Express is exploring reimbursement for some agent mistakes, while banks build their own AI tools.

97cd20591521.headline: Google Wires Target and Grocery Chains Into Search and Gemini Before the Holiday Rush
body: Google has added four new grocery Connected Apps to Google Search and the Gemini app, just as holiday shopping season ramps up, according to Digital Trends. The new additions are Albertsons, Safeway, Shaw's and Target, and they join Instacart, which had been the only grocery option and arrived in Search in July.

The idea is simple: instead of bouncing between store websites, you ask Google to help build a grocery order and then check out. The integrations run on the Universal Commerce Protocol, and Target was one of the retailers that helped develop that protocol earlier this year. For now the grocery apps are available only in the US.

Using them takes a few steps. You need to be signed into a Google Account, and many apps require linking your account first. Connecting is optional and can be undone later from your Google Account settings. You can summon an app by naming it or by starting your request with @ and the service name. In Search, Connected Apps currently work in AI Mode, and Google has said it plans to bring them to AI Overviews too.

Groceries are not the only category getting the treatment. Experian, long available in Gemini, has now arrived in Search so US users can check their credit rating and shop for a personal loan. H&R Block is available in Search for tax calculations and refund estimates.

In the coming weeks, Angi and Thumbtack are also expected to let users link accounts to Search. Google says that should make it easier to find a local pro, say for a dripping tap during last-minute holiday prep.
97cd20591521.summary: Google added Albertsons, Safeway, Shaw's and Target as grocery Connected Apps in Search and Gemini in the US, alongside Instacart. Credit and tax tools are also expanding, with Angi and Thumbtack coming soon.
97cd20591521.pixel_take: Google now wants to be your shopping list, your credit check and your plumber's phone book. The turkey is still your problem, though.
97cd20591521.why_it_matters: Google is turning Search and Gemini into places where transactions happen, not just where people look things up. That could shift where retailers compete for shoppers and how much data flows through one company. For consumers, it may save time, but linking accounts deserves a moment of thought.
key_points: Albertsons, Safeway, Shaw's and Target join Instacart as grocery Connected Apps in Search and Gemini.
The apps run on the Universal Commerce Protocol and are US-only for now.
Experian and H&R Block are in Search, with Angi and Thumbtack coming in weeks.

e617de6ab327.headline: Onchain FX may grow from real users first, not Wall Street-sized liquidity
body: A Cointelegraph piece published on November 22, 2026 argues that onchain foreign exchange does not have to replicate the huge institutional currency market before it becomes useful. According to the outlet, real user demand could let smaller markets work first.

That is a notable change in framing. The traditional FX market is enormous, often described as the largest financial market in the world, and it is built on deep liquidity from banks and large institutions. Trying to match that on a blockchain from day one would be like opening a lemonade stand and asking it to compete with a global supermarket chain.

The teaser's argument is that usefulness does not depend on scale at the start. If people actually need to swap currencies onchain, for payments, transfers or everyday use, that demand can bring in liquidity gradually, rather than waiting for institutions to show up first.

The full text of the article was not available to us, so details such as specific platforms, currencies or figures are not covered here. What the headline and teaser make clear is the thesis: build around users, and the liquidity can follow.

This echoes a familiar pattern in technology, where products often start with a niche of committed users and expand from there instead of launching at full institutional scale. Whether onchain FX follows that path will depend on whether genuine demand shows up.
e617de6ab327.summary: A Cointelegraph piece argues onchain foreign exchange can become useful by serving real user demand in smaller markets first, without needing to recreate the trillion-dollar institutional FX market.
e617de6ab327.pixel_take: Onchain FX is saying it doesn't need to be the ocean on day one. A well-used pond beats an empty ocean, and nobody has to pretend otherwise.
e617de6ab327.why_it_matters: Currency conversion touches anyone who sends money abroad, travels or trades across borders. If onchain FX can grow from real use, it could eventually offer alternatives to traditional channels. The bottom-up approach also hints at where crypto infrastructure may find practical traction.
key_points: Cointelegraph argues onchain FX need not copy the trillion-dollar institutional market.
Real user demand could make smaller markets viable first.
The full article text was unavailable, so specifics are limited.

d619d9b762e9.headline: P&G Plans More 'Lights-Out' Factory Shifts, Where Pampers Get Made Without Humans
body: Procter & Gamble, the maker of Pampers and Bounty paper towels, plans to expand the number of factory shifts that run without human workers on site, according to The New York Times. The goal is to cut costs.

The company currently operates 15 sites capable of running shifts unattended, the report says, and it plans to add more in 2027. The material available does not say how many sites will be added, how much money P&G expects to save, or what the change means for its workforce.

The idea is often called 'lights-out' manufacturing: automated machines keep producing while the building is effectively left to the robots. For a company that makes high-volume household staples, the appeal is easy to see. Machines do not need breaks, and they can keep a production line humming through overnight or off-peak hours.

The move also fits a wider pattern. Consumer goods makers have spent years looking for ways to protect profit margins when raw materials, transport and labor all cost more, and when shoppers push back on price increases. Automation is one of the few levers that can lower costs without raising shelf prices.

Questions remain about the human side of the equation. Unattended shifts typically still depend on technicians, engineers and maintenance crews for other parts of the day, but the details of P&G's plans were not available in the material we reviewed. We will be watching for more from the company.
d619d9b762e9.summary: Procter & Gamble, maker of Pampers and Bounty, runs 15 sites able to operate shifts without humans and plans to add more in 2027, aiming to cut costs, according to The New York Times.
d619d9b762e9.pixel_take: Your diapers and paper towels may soon be made by a night shift that never asks for a coffee break, never calls in sick, and never steals the good stapler.
d619d9b762e9.why_it_matters: Automation at a giant consumer goods maker signals how big companies hope to protect margins without simply hiking prices. For shoppers, it could mean steadier prices on everyday items; for workers, it raises questions about which factory jobs remain.
key_points: P&G has 15 sites able to run shifts with no humans present.
The company plans to add more such sites in 2027.
The stated aim is to cut manufacturing costs.

be824d35f3bd.headline: Anthropic reportedly ran a SpaceX-style IPO process, and some bankers are not thrilled
body: Anthropic ran an unusual process for its initial public offering, similar to the approach taken by SpaceX, and the unconventional route has chafed some bankers, according to an exclusive report published by Investing.com on November 22, 2026.

The material available for this story is limited to the headline, so details such as the structure of the process, the banks involved, the size of the deal or the timeline are not confirmed here. What the headline does establish is that Anthropic's approach resembled the one used by SpaceX and that it ruffled feathers among some of the bankers involved.

Some context helps. A traditional IPO usually follows a well-worn script: banks are hired to underwrite the deal, they run roadshows, gather investor demand and collect fees for the privilege. Companies that depart from that script can shift leverage away from Wall Street and toward the issuer, which is rarely popular with the people who earn a living from the script.

That explains the grumbling. Underwriting fees and the prestige of leading a blockbuster listing are significant prizes for banks, and any process that changes who gets which role, or how much, tends to produce unhappy bankers.

For investors, the takeaway is that the biggest listings of the AI era may not follow the standard playbook. How such deals are priced and allocated can influence first-day trading, who gets access to shares and how smoothly the stock settles after debut. More details should emerge as the full report circulates.
be824d35f3bd.summary: Investing.com reports that Anthropic ran an unconventional IPO process, like SpaceX did, and some bankers were irritated by it. Few details are available beyond the headline.
be824d35f3bd.pixel_take: When your IPO skips the usual script, the bankers who wrote the script start sighing loudly. Wall Street hates a plot twist, especially one that touches the fee schedule.
be824d35f3bd.why_it_matters: How blockbuster IPOs are run affects who gets shares, how they are priced and what banks earn. If top AI and space companies keep bypassing the traditional playbook, it could reshape Wall Street's role in major listings and the access ordinary investors get.
key_points: Anthropic reportedly ran an unusual IPO process, similar to SpaceX's
Some bankers were reportedly unhappy with the approach
Details of the structure and deal are not in the available material

2b86c9cc5f29.headline: Iran shows off dual-missile launcher and underground 'missile city' while a US naval blockade squeezes its economy
body: Iran has put its upgraded missile arsenal on display, with state media airing footage of commanders touring an underground missile facility on Saturday. According to Al Jazeera, the showcase included a launcher built to fire two liquid-fuelled missiles at once, part of a message that Iran remains militarily capable despite US-Israeli attacks.

Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, led the tour, state broadcaster IRIB reported. Footage showed kilometres of tunnels and hundreds of missiles and launchers, including double launchers. IRIB said liquid-fuelled missiles launch vertically and allow speed control, which can help them get past air defences. State media also claimed newer missiles have better range and accuracy, plus guidance that does not depend on US GPS.

The tour followed an IRGC aerospace force announcement on November 10 of a new underground facility, according to the semiofficial Tasnim agency. Tasnim said Iran is building underground complexes that can keep making and storing weapons under heavy bombardment, and the IRGC says it has moved missile and drone production from the surface to underground sites. Al Jazeera's Resul Serdar noted it was unclear when the footage was filmed.

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera see a strategic signal. Serdar called it propaganda but also an attempt to restore deterrence. Rami Khouri of the American University of Beirut said underground sites can hold spare parts, raw materials and chemicals as well as finished weapons, and that Iran has planned for this for decades.

The politics add another layer. Rob Geist Pinfold of King's College London said Iran feels emboldened after Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered sweeping midterm losses, in which the rising cost of living from the war was a major factor. He argued Tehran sees a US reluctant to escalate.

Yet Iran is under real strain. A US naval blockade of its southern ports has disrupted oil exports, and Pinfold said very little oil, if any, is leaving the country. He said the economy is already in recession and could take a bigger hit, which may push Tehran to escalate because it feels cornered.
2b86c9cc5f29.summary: Iran showcased a dual-missile launcher and an underground missile facility in a show of strength, even as a US naval blockade cuts its oil exports and pushes its economy deeper into recession, according to Al Jazeera.
2b86c9cc5f29.why_it_matters: Iran's oil exports are largely cut off, and any renewed fighting could rattle energy markets and prices. The war's cost-of-living effects already influenced US elections, showing how geopolitics reaches household budgets.
key_points: Iran displayed a launcher able to fire two liquid-fuelled missiles at once, plus underground tunnels holding hundreds of missiles.
Analysts see the display as an effort to restore deterrence, though it is unclear when the footage was filmed.
A US naval blockade has sharply reduced Iranian oil exports, and the economy is already in recession.

9f6df889b722.headline: House Democrats Torn: Defund the Iran War Now or Wait Until They Hold the Purse Strings?
body: House Democrats are divided over how to handle funding for the war with Iran during the lame-duck session, according to The Hill. The debate is whether to demand an end to war funding now, or to push that fight into next year.

The risk of acting now is a government shutdown. Tying a funding cutoff to must-pass spending legislation in the final weeks of the current Congress could trigger a lapse in government funding if the two sides cannot agree.

The alternative is patience. The Hill reports that Democrats will control Congress next year, which would give them far more leverage over any war spending. Waiting would mean postponing the confrontation until they hold the majority, rather than forcing it with the current balance of power.

The source material available is limited to the headline and teaser, so details on how many Democrats favor each approach, who is leading each camp, and the specific legislation involved are not available. What is clear is that the party is weighing a classic dilemma: make a bold stand immediately, or save the fight for when it can be won more easily.

Congress's power of the purse is its most direct tool over military action, and funding fights are where wars are often debated in earnest. How Democrats choose to use it, and when, will shape both the war's future and the political cost of any shutdown.
9f6df889b722.summary: House Democrats are split on whether to demand an end to Iran war funding in the lame-duck session, risking a shutdown, or to wait until they control Congress next year, The Hill reports.
9f6df889b722.why_it_matters: A shutdown fight can disrupt federal paychecks, services and contracts, and rattle markets that dislike budget uncertainty. Decisions on war funding also affect defense spending, and the timing of this fight could shape government finances well into next year.
key_points: House Democrats are divided over lame-duck strategy on the Iran war.
One option is demanding an end to war funding now, risking a government shutdown.
The other is delaying the fight until next year, when Democrats will control Congress.

82a8a10f0807.headline: Apple's HomeView Is a Fine Speaker and a Great Jukebox, Until CarPlay Apps Show Up
body: The Verge has published a follow-up to its review of Apple's HomeView, the company's first smart display, answering reader questions about how it works as a smart speaker. The verdict: it sounds decent for its size and works well as a touchscreen music controller, but third-party audio apps are a mess.

On sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini than to a full-size HomePod or a Sonos One. Against the Mini 2, The Verge found the tabletop HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but is less clear and fills a room less well. The display sits over the speaker base and partly covers it, so Apple added an accelerometer that adjusts the EQ as you tilt the screen. It supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 does not. The wall-mounted version has only two drivers and almost no bass, so it is better for talking to a visitor through a video doorbell than for music.

There is no stereo pairing, either. You can group HomeViews with other AirPlay speakers, but you can't pair two together or pair one with a HomePod or Mini. The reviewer's advice is that for $300 and good sound, two Minis in stereo beat a HomeView. The screen is the real draw, acting like a jukebox for changing songs, picking music and browsing podcasts or audiobooks without voice commands.

Handoff works much as on HomePods. In testing it worked with Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Pocket Casts, YouTube Music, FaceTime and phone calls, though calls sometimes dropped. Netflix and Amazon Prime Video handed off audio only, though video played in Safari. Handoff is also aggressive if your phone is within a few inches.

The biggest complaint is third-party apps. Instead of building a dedicated HomeView experience, Apple reuses its CarPlay platform, so any audio or video app that supports CarPlay already works. The cost is no search box or keyboard, slower and laggier performance, and a need for your phone and profile on the same Wi-Fi, so only you can use them. The Verge also hit bugs: control screens that didn't appear and an Audible app that often refused to load. Siri also defaults to the HomeView's own speaker for these apps rather than your last-used speakers.

The takeaway: buy a HomeView if you want a touchscreen music controller and use Apple Music, which is the only service anyone in the house can use. If you mostly use Spotify or other apps, or are happy with voice and phone control, a HomePod is the safer pick. The Verge says CarPlay support feels like a stopgap that Apple needs to refine with developers.
82a8a10f0807.summary: The Verge's follow-up finds Apple's HomeView sounds close to a HomePod Mini and works well as a touchscreen music controller, but CarPlay-based third-party apps like Spotify and Audible are slow, buggy and lack search.
82a8a10f0807.pixel_take: Apple built a kitchen jukebox, then loaded it with apps that warn you to be stationary before watching video. Good news: the fridge isn't going anywhere.
82a8a10f0807.why_it_matters: Apple's shortcut of reusing CarPlay shows how platform makers can trade polish for speed, which affects how useful a $300 gadget really is. For shoppers, the choice between a smart display and cheaper speakers depends on which music service you actually use.
key_points: HomeView sounds closest to a HomePod Mini: more bass and louder, but less clear and less room-filling.
Third-party apps run through CarPlay, so they lack search, are slower and need a user profile.
Only Apple Music can be used by anyone in the household; two Minis beat HomeView for sound at $300.

8169d7dc0073.headline: Bitcoin Flashes $17K on Kraken, and the Exchange Says the Trades Stand
body: Bitcoin briefly dropped to $17,000 on the crypto exchange Kraken, according to Cointelegraph, and the exchange said the trades that executed during the dip will stand. The report was published on November 22, 2026.

Kraken said all orders were processed correctly. The exchange also said it found no evidence of a security breach or of compromised accounts, which rules out the most worrying explanations for a sudden price plunge.

The material available does not say what caused the drop, how long it lasted, or how many traders were affected, so those questions remain open. What is clear is Kraken's position: the market worked as designed, and the prices that printed are the prices that count.

Sudden price spikes and dips on a single venue are not new in crypto. Thin order books, forced liquidations or a large sell order can push a price far from where it trades elsewhere for a few moments. Exchanges then face a choice between honoring the trades and reversing them, and each option leaves someone unhappy.

Upholding trades means buyers who snagged coins at a steep discount keep them, while holders who were sold out at the bottom do not get a do-over. Reversing trades protects the unlucky but raises fairness questions about changing the rules after the fact. Kraken has chosen the first path, at least according to the headline and teaser.
8169d7dc0073.summary: Bitcoin briefly fell to $17,000 on Kraken, per Cointelegraph. The exchange says all orders were processed correctly, found no security breach or compromised accounts, and is keeping the trades in place.
8169d7dc0073.pixel_take: Bitcoin took a brief trip to the clearance rack, and Kraken's message to anyone who got caught is that the receipts are final.
8169d7dc0073.why_it_matters: Flash dips on one exchange can trigger stop-losses and liquidations, so how a platform handles them affects real money. Kraken's refusal to reverse trades is a reminder that in crypto, the execution price is usually final, whatever the cause.
key_points: Bitcoin briefly hit $17,000 on Kraken, according to Cointelegraph.
Kraken says all orders were processed correctly and the trades stand.
The exchange found no evidence of a security breach or compromised accounts.

bddb5ebd608e.headline: Your Old Console Might Be a Jackpot: 10 Rare Editions Collectors Chase
body: Engadget has published a roundup of rare game consoles, and the message is that the dusty box in your closet might be worth checking. Limited editions, sweepstakes prizes and region-locked bundles from Nintendo, Sony, Sega and Microsoft have sold for far more than their original prices, according to the outlet.

Some of the numbers are striking. A gold Nintendo 64, a Toys "R" Us exclusive, appears only nine times in Video Game Authority's December 2025 census. A graded example with two controllers sold for $3,250 in January 2026. The Pikachu Edition N64, sealed and graded, reached $16,250 in August 2026, though Engadget notes those are complete collector sets, not typical used consoles. A loose one is estimated near $390.

Sony's rarities include the Midnight Blue PlayStation from a 2000 sweepstakes, with a reported 200 consoles across North America and Japan. Prices are hard to pin down, but one 10 Million model sold on eBay for $10,326.32 in October 2024. Panasonic's Q, a GameCube with a built-in DVD player, launched in Japan in 2001 and is now estimated at about $1,645 loose.

Sega is represented by the Saturn Skeleton Edition, limited to 30,000 units, and two Dreamcasts. The Maziora Edition reportedly had only 500 units, and the Resident Evil Code: Veronica bundle had 2,000 total, just 200 in blue. One blue unit is currently listed for $18,000, though listings are not sales.

Microsoft's entries include the Japan-only Pure White Xbox, limited to 1,000 units, with complete sets selling for roughly $1,600 to $2,650 in 2026. A newer pick is the 2018 PS4 Pro 500 Million Limited Edition, with 50,000 made, which has sold for $500 to $750. The list also includes the Xbox Launch Team Edition, made for the people behind the original console and signed with Bill Gates' name.
Engadget's caveat is worth heeding: condition, packaging, accessories and grading matter enormously, and some variants lack enough sales data for a reliable price.
bddb5ebd608e.summary: Engadget rounded up 10 rare consoles, from a gold N64 to a Japan-only Xbox, that have resold for far above launch prices. Condition, packaging and grading drive values.
bddb5ebd608e.pixel_take: Forget index funds: somewhere a translucent Saturn is quietly outperforming your portfolio, as long as you kept the box and never once played it.
bddb5ebd608e.why_it_matters: Collectible hardware has become a real alternative asset, with documented auction sales and price guides setting values. For readers, it shows that scarcity, condition and original packaging can matter more than age, but prices vary widely and listings are not the same as completed sales.
key_points: Limited runs range from nine graded gold N64s to 50,000 PS4 Pro units.
A sealed, graded Pikachu N64 sold for $16,250 in August 2026, but loose units are far cheaper.
Some rarities, like the Maziora Dreamcast, lack enough sales data for reliable pricing.

113d0aee3c51.headline: Stocks Had a Rough Week, but an Old Seasonal Timing Model Smells a Bounce
body: After a brutal week for the market, a well-known timing tool is flashing a more upbeat signal. According to MarketWatch, Norm Fosback's 'Seasonality Timing System' suggests stocks have an upside bias over the next two weeks.

MarketWatch describes the system as having one of the very best long-term track records among market timing models. The framing is that history, at least the calendar kind, is leaning in the market's favor after the recent sell-off.

The material available is just a headline and teaser, so details of the model's rules, its historical returns and the size of last week's losses are not part of what we can report. We won't invent them, and you shouldn't assume them either.

Some context helps. Seasonality models rest on the idea that markets tend to behave differently at certain times of the calendar, such as around month-ends, holidays or the turn of a month. Investors have studied these patterns for decades, and some of them have held up better than others.

The caveat is the usual one: a tendency is not a guarantee. A two-week upside bias means the odds may be modestly better, not that a rebound is booked like a table at a restaurant. Seasonal signals can be swamped by news, earnings, interest rate expectations or plain old panic.

For everyday investors, the sensible takeaway is probably not to trade on a calendar quirk. It is a reminder that rough weeks often feel like the start of something worse, while historical patterns sometimes say the mood may be gloomier than the odds.
113d0aee3c51.summary: MarketWatch reports that Norm Fosback's Seasonality Timing System, known for a strong long-term record, points to an upside bias for stocks over the next two weeks after a rough week.
113d0aee3c51.pixel_take: The market had a terrible week, and the calendar is basically saying, 'There, there.' Just remember that seasonal patterns are a nudge, not a promise.
113d0aee3c51.why_it_matters: Sell-offs tempt investors into rash moves, and timing models like this offer a data-driven counterweight to panic. Still, a seasonal tilt is only one input, so it should not replace diversification or a long-term plan for your money.
key_points: Norm Fosback's Seasonality Timing System is cited as having a top-tier long-term record.
It suggests an upside bias for stocks over the next two weeks, per MarketWatch.
The signal follows a brutal week for the market and is a tendency, not a guarantee.

3e2b016a40c9.headline: Democrats Eye a December Funding Fight to Force an End to the Iran War, Vietnam-Style
body: Some Democrats in Congress want to use a December 11 government funding deadline to try to force President Donald Trump to end the US-Israel war on Iran, according to Al Jazeera. The tactic carries a real risk: if the package fails, a government shutdown would begin on December 12.

The push follows this month's midterm elections, where Democrats ran on ending the conflict and won majorities in both the House and the Senate. They take control on January 3, but Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna argue that waiting is too slow. In a joint statement they urged colleagues to oppose any funding package that does not explicitly bar money for offensive operations in Iran. Senators Chris Van Hollen, Tammy Duckworth, Michael Bennet and Bernie Sanders backed similar language.

The historical model is Vietnam. In June 1973 Congress passed the Case-Church Amendment, cutting off federal funds for the war, with veto-proof support of more than two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers. Congress also overrode Nixon's veto of the War Powers Resolution that November. South Vietnam's government in Saigon fell in April 1975.

The numbers today are tougher. Republicans control Congress for another six weeks, and even in the next Congress Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats against the 67 needed to override a veto, and 257 House seats against the 290 required. Democrats have forced more than 15 war powers votes without success. A House resolution passed 220-204 in September with seven Republican votes, but Senate Republicans blocked it 51-48 last week.

The party is also split on tactics. Rosa DeLauro, set to chair the House Appropriations Committee, supports cutting off war funds but has not backed a shutdown and prefers a short-term extension over a year-long package. She questioned whether Americans would believe a shutdown ends the war. Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer have not taken a position. Republicans, while acknowledging the war's high costs, say the US must finish the job.
There is also an economic worry: critics fear a shutdown would pile onto already soaring food and petrol prices.
3e2b016a40c9.summary: Some Democrats want to attach an Iran war funding ban to the December 11 spending deadline, echoing Vietnam-era cutoffs. Party divisions, veto math and shutdown risks complicate the plan.
3e2b016a40c9.why_it_matters: A shutdown starting December 12 would disrupt federal agencies at a time when food and petrol prices are already climbing. The fight also shows how war spending and congressional leverage can shape budgets, markets and household costs.
key_points: Democrats are eyeing the December 11 funding deadline to bar money for offensive operations in Iran, risking a shutdown on December 12.
They lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a Trump veto, even in the next Congress.
Party leaders are split, with DeLauro favoring a short-term extension and Jeffries and Schumer undecided.
